new.title: Direct inference of cosmological mass growth via timing of black hole - pulsar binaries
new.summary: Cosmologically coupled black holes (CCBHs) respond to the expansion of the Universe, independently of conventional astrophysical processes. Recent CCBH solutions in General Relativity demonstrate evolution of gravitating mass $m_{\rm BH}\propto a^\kappa$, where $a$ is the cosmological scale factor. This can be tested through the orbital period timing of black hole (BH) pulsar (PSR) binaries. In contrast to previous methods used to constrain $\kappa$, pulsar timing measurement baselines span decades instead of gigayears, allowing sources of bias to be well-controlled. As a test case, we analyze the globular cluster BH+PSR candidate J0514--4002E (spin $P\sim 5.6~{\rm ms}$, orbital period $P_{\rm b}\sim 7~\rm days$) under the assumption that the companion is a CCBH. Taking the difference between the observed orbital and spin period derivatives removes all kinematic effects, leaving only the pulsar's intrinsic spin-down $\dot{P}_{\rm int}$ as unknown. Setting $\dot{P}_{\rm int} = 0$, its physical minimum, gives a robust upper bound $\kappa \leqslant 3.95$ at $95\%$ confidence. We estimate $\dot{P}_{\rm int}$ through the population of millisecond pulsars matched in spin and infer $\kappa = 0.82 \pm 1.67$ and $0.75 \pm 1.54$, using $H_0 = 67.6$ and $73.5\,{\rm km\,s^{-1}\,Mpc^{-1}}$, respectively. Adopting typical baseline scaling of timing precision, the value $\kappa = 3$, argued elsewhere to link energized vacuum BH interiors to accelerated cosmological expansion, can be excluded or detected for this $2.35^{+0.20}_{-0.18}\,M_\odot$ companion at $3\sigma$ and $5\sigma$ confidence by 2031 and 2036, respectively.

new.title: Spiral Pitch Angles in Black Hole Images and Movies
new.summary: The Event Horizon Telescope (EHT) has produced images of M87* and Sgr A*, and will soon produce time sequences of images, or movies. General relativistic magnetohydrodynamics (GRMHD) models predict EHT sources will exhibit brightness fluctuations along the ring. The fluctuations are commonly connected to trailing spiral features. Here, we introduce a method to measure the pitch angle $\psi$ of radially extended features by cross-correlating brightness fluctuations sampled on rings at two distinct impact parameters. Pitch angle can be reliably measured from synthetic movies with BHEX resolution, and can be constrained even at EHT resolution. Single images enable noisy constraints of $\psi$. Pitch angle depends most on the viewing inclination and black hole spin. For constant inclination, the spiral winding direction depends on the sign of spin, with spirals winding more tightly in the direction of frame dragging near the horizon. The pitch angle will complement other observables to reliably constrain both the source inclination and spin in future analysis by EHT, and by expansions to the EHT such as ngEHT and BHEX.

new.title: Intra-day variability of the gamma-ray/optical emission of 3C 454.3: the complexity beyond the long-term correlation
new.summary: Simultaneous $\gamma$-ray/optical observations probe particle acceleration and radiative processes in blazar jets. The blazar 3C 454.3 shows a significant long-term correlation between these bands, often interpreted as support for the canonical one-zone leptonic emission model. However, both bands show strong intra-day variability, and whether the correlation persists during individual flares remains unclear. We study the $\gamma$-ray/optical correlation and intra-day variability of 3C 454.3 over 17 years (2007--2024), on timescales $\leq 24$ h. We analyse AGILE and Fermi-LAT observations using light curves binned from 3 to 48 h, together with simultaneous $R$-band photometry from WEBT and public optical data sets. We examine the flux and spectral evolution of individual flares, estimate time-dependent correlation properties, and derive Compton dominance from optical and $\gamma$-ray luminosities. We confirm the long-term correlation, but find large intrinsic dispersion and a slope of $\eta \simeq 1.6$--$1.7$, inconsistent with a single canonical one-zone scenario. On shorter timescales, correlation strengths range from weak to strong, with slopes spanning $\eta \simeq 0.4$--$2.0$. We also find orphan flares in both bands, diverse flare morphologies, distinct Compton-dominance patterns with rapid excursions from $\sim 10$ to 120, and heterogeneous spectral trends. The shortest resolved variability timescales ($t_{\rm var} \lesssim 3$ h) indicate that localized emission regions are required by causality. The $\gamma$-ray/optical correlation in 3C 454.3 thus arises not from a single emission regime, but from multiple epoch-dependent physical states. Increasing temporal resolution reveals richer variability, highlighting the importance of systematic intra-day, multi-epoch studies of bright FSRQs.

new.title: FAST Burst-Cluster Catalog of FRB 20240114A
new.summary: We present the complete FAST burst-cluster catalog of FRB 20240114A, covering its 495-day active episode from January 28, 2024 to June 5, 2025. The catalog contains 13261 burst clusters, 19037 bursts, and 29026 sub-bursts detected in 99 observing sessions. The data reveal distinct organization across temporal scales. Among drifting burst clusters, downward-drifting clusters outnumber upward-drifting ones by approximately $9.4:1$. Between separate burst clusters, previously reported frequency changes show no preferred direction, while our Weibull analysis finds their arrival times broadly consistent with Poisson statistics, suggesting that burst clusters may represent approximately independent emission episodes within observing sessions. The Parkes/Murriyang observations revealed a long-term modulation of the characteristic emission frequency, and the extended FAST measurements show a consistent evolution. Burst energetics increase with cluster multiplicity and activity level, although significant scatter remains. The manually refined dispersion measure increases at $1.29\pm0.11\,\mathrm{pc\,cm^{-3}\,yr^{-1}}$, enlarging the still limited but growing sample of repeaters with increasing DM. Overall, these results summarize the spectral--temporal evolution of FRB 20240114A and present a burst-cluster catalog linked to the existing BurstID measurements, providing a basis for future studies of repeating FRBs.

new.title: A Shallow Phase-resolved Gamma-Ray Luminosity-Cutoff Energy Relation in Globular Cluster Millisecond Pulsars
new.summary: Globular clusters (GCs) provide dense stellar environments for investigating the high-energy emission of millisecond pulsars (MSPs). Using $\sim$17.3~yr of \textit{Fermi}-LAT Pass~8 data in the 0.1-500.0~GeV range, we study four MSPs that dominate, or contribute substantially to, the GeV $\gamma$-ray emission of their host GCs. Significant off-pulse $\gamma$-ray emission is detected from PSR~J1823$-$3021A, J1824$-$2452A, and J1835$-$3259B. For these sources, the cutoff energy, $E_{\rm cut}$, varies systematically with rotational phase and is positively correlated with the phase-resolved energy flux. Using the phase-resolved isotropic $\gamma$-ray luminosity ($L_{\gamma}$), we find $L_{\gamma}\propto E_{\rm cut}^{\alpha}$ with $\alpha=0.74^{+0.16}_{-0.14}$. This slope is substantially shallower than that reported for field MSPs, $\alpha=2.31^{+0.22}_{-0.25}$, and the $\alpha=16/7\simeq2.29$ scaling expected for curvature radiation in the equatorial current sheet framework. The origin of the shallow relation remains uncertain, potentially reflecting cluster-associated $\gamma$-ray emission, differences in emission geometry and beaming, or limited photon statistics. Our results demonstrate that GC MSPs provide valuable targets for testing phase-resolved high-energy emission physics in dense stellar environments.

new.title: False Periodicities in Repeating Fast Radio Bursts Caused by Burst Clustering
new.summary: Fast radio bursts (FRBs) are millisecond-duration radio transients with high brightness temperatures, but their physical origin remains uncertain. The association of FRB 200428 with a Galactic magnetar provides compelling evidence that at least some FRBs originate from magnetar-like systems. Nevertheless, periodic modulation associated with neutron-star rotation has not been robustly detected in extragalactic FRBs. Motivated by the reported 1.7 s periodicity in the active repeater FRB 20201124A, we conduct a systematic search for short-timescale periodicity in four highly active repeating FRB sources. We employ a sliding-window method that analyzes temporally adjacent bursts within restricted time intervals, allowing transient or intermittent periodic signals to be identified. The search yields apparent period candidates with nominal Poisson-calibrated significances comparable to that reported for the 1.7 s signal, although the inferred periods vary substantially among sources and observing windows. We then perform a nonparametric waiting-time randomization test, in which the observed waiting-time distribution is preserved while the temporal ordering is destroyed. The randomized sequences reproduce the main candidate-period structures seen in the data, demonstrating that these apparent periodicities can arise from the non-Poissonian waiting-time statistics rather than from a coherent periodic process. Rotation-modulated epidemic-type aftershock sequence simulations provide a complementary parametric illustration of the same effect. We therefore find no robust evidence for a short intrinsic periodicity in these data, and the reported 1.7 s signal is not uniquely distinguished from clustering-induced candidates. Robust periodicity searches must evaluate significance against null models that account for the observed waiting-time statistics and the full search procedure.

new.title: New Candidate Activity Periods from FRB 20240209A and Repeating Fast Radio Burst Sources in the Second CHIME/FRB Catalog
new.summary: Repeating fast radio burst (FRB) sources with periodic activity provide important constraints on FRB models invoking neutron-star precession, rotation, or orbital modulation in binary systems. Although a few FRB sources exhibit evidence of periodic behavior, it remains unclear whether periodic activity is a common underlying feature of repeating FRBs. Using a new FRB periodicity search pipeline introduced by A. B. Pearlman et al. (2026), which is optimized for sparse event-arrival-time data from FRB surveys, we search for activity periods in the burst arrival times from FRB 20240209A and repeating FRBs in the Second Canadian Hydrogen Intensity Mapping Experiment (CHIME)/FRB Catalog. For FRB 20240209A, we identify a new candidate activity period of 170.4 $\pm$ 4.7 days, with a trials-corrected statistical significance of 5.3$\sigma$. Our larger burst sample shows no evidence of the 128.5-day activity period previously reported for this source by A. Pal (2025). We also report candidate activity periods of 28.46 $\pm$ 0.08 days, 86.7 $\pm$ 0.5 days, and 36.4 $\pm$ 0.5 days for FRB 20190208A, FRB 20200926A, and FRB 20220529A, with trials-corrected statistical significances of 3.1$\sigma$, 4.0$\sigma$, and 3.5$\sigma$, respectively. All statistical significances are evaluated against a homogeneous (constant-rate) Poisson null hypothesis, and we caution that they may decrease under null models that incorporate burst clustering. Collectively, our results constitute the most comprehensive search for periodic activity in the repeating FRB population to date.

new.title: The origin of the apparent ULX deficit in NGC 3256
new.summary: Ultra-luminous X-ray (ULX) sources are bright, off-nuclear X-ray point sources, mostly associated with high-mass X-ray binaries (HMXBs), with a compact object accreting from a donor star at super-Eddington luminosities. Although their HMXB nature implies a connection to star formation processes, previous works have found that luminous infrared galaxies (LIRGs) appear to have a deficit of ULXs compared to their very high star formation rates (SFRs). Here, we analyze three Chandra observations of NGC 3256, a merging LIRG with SFR ~50-60 Msun/yr. Based on local scaling relations, it could be expected to host between 100-120 individual ULXs, which could have a non-negligible impact on the energetics and feedback processes of the galaxy. We aim to characterize all its detected X-ray point sources to determine if there is a ULX deficit in this galaxy. We also aim to explore the potential impact of host-galaxy obscuration and metallicity in said deficit. We characterize the luminosity of each X-ray point source in each Chandra observation, and use all observations to determine their potential ULX nature and the fraction of transient ULXs, as well as construct a ULX luminosity function for this galaxy. We find that the galaxy hosts 10-15 ULXs, making it one of the most ULX-rich galaxies known to date. While comparison with the ULX/SFR ratio of nearby galaxies predicted as many as ~100 ULXs, we show that, when accounting for its very high metallicity, NGC 3256 does not have a ULX deficit; and may even present an excess. While the high obscuration in LIRGs has previously been invoked to explain the ULX deficit, we conclude that it is not required to explain the ULX to SFR ratio in NGC 3256. If obscuration still plays a role, then LIRGs may actually be significantly more efficient at producing ULXs than normal galaxies (of the same metallicity), in disagreement with previous results.

new.title: Gamma-Ray Bursts from Primordial Black Hole-Induced Neutron Star Collapse
new.summary: We show that the capture and subsequent endoparasitic consumption of a neutron star (NS) by a primordial black hole (PBH) can produce a short gamma-ray burst (GRB) without forming an accretion disk. During PBH-induced NS consumption, the NS spin is amplified through angular-momentum conservation and transfer from infalling matter, while flux freezing and a differential-rotation-driven dynamo amplify the magnetic field. We find that, for rapidly rotating millisecond pulsars (MSPs), these mechanisms can power short GRBs through magnetic dipole radiation and magnetic energy release. If asteroid-mass PBHs in the range $10^{-14}M_\odot$--$10^{-11}M_\odot$ constitute the dark matter, we estimate that searches of the Fermi-GBM archive and a future MeV gamma-ray mission such as COSI could detect these bursts. We also discuss possible multimessenger counterparts, including fast radio bursts powered by magnetic energy release, kilonovae and $511\,{\rm keV}$ line emission associated with centrifugally ejected neutron-rich matter, and gravitational waves from the rapid collapse and subsequent black-hole ringdown. Together, these signals probe complementary stages of PBH-induced NS consumption.

new.title: Fast X-Ray Transients from Dense Circumstellar Material Shock Breakout and Cooling Emission
new.summary: In this Letter, we explore the soft X-ray shock breakout (SBO) and cooling emission of supernovae interacting with pre-explosion dense circumstellar material (CSM) shells as a subclass of extragalactic fast X-ray transients. For geometrically thin CSM shells, we find that the SBO luminosities span a range of a few $10^{43}-10^{45}\,{\rm{erg}}\,{\rm{s}}^{-1}$, with peak times typically $\lesssim10^4\,{\rm{s}}$, both of which are primarily determined by the light-travel effect. When the shell's outer radius is located at $\sim100-500\,R_\odot$, the SBO temperatures fall into the energy band covered by the current soft X-ray facilities. We derive analytic lightcurves for SBOs in dense CSM shells and explore how different physical parameters affect the observed lightcurves and the temperature evolution. Despite the multi-temperature nature of the emission caused by the light-travel effect leading to non-thermal-like spectra, we find that the time-resolved spectra within the limited soft X-ray band can still be well described by a blackbody model. This provides a natural explanation for the observed blackbody-like time-resolved spectra of soft X-ray SBO events. Our model can reproduce the observed X-ray lightcurves and temperature evolutions of the three known X-ray SBO events, EP260321a, XRF\,060218, and XRO\,080109, revealing a diversity in the properties of the dense CSM shells ejected by stripped-envelope progenitors before the explosion. Future discoveries of more soft X-ray SBO events by facilities such as Einstein Probe will provide opportunities for probing the episodic mass-loss history of massive stars in the final stages before core collapse.

new.title: Strong Field Tidal Disruptions of Rotating Stars by Spinning Black Holes
new.summary: We study tidal disruptions of rotating solar-type stars by a rapidly spinning supermassive black hole with general-relativistic smoothed-particle hydrodynamics. To capture strong-field effects, we place the pericentre at a few gravitational radii of a black hole, and compare with weak-field encounters at a larger pericentre around a lighter black hole. We vary the black hole spin, the orbital inclination and the stellar rotation, using rigidly and differentially rotating stars with spin aligned, anti-aligned or perpendicular to the orbital angular momentum. In the strong field, the black hole spin decides whether a core survives on equatorial and inclined orbits, and stellar rotation reduces the surviving core in every partial disruption. At the larger pericentre, as in Newtonian studies, anti-aligned rotation instead protects the star from disruption. In both cases the tide reverses an anti-aligned spin just before pericentre. The outcome differs because in the strong field the tide keeps acting on the reversed core long after pericentre. Deep encounters leave cores spinning above break-up, which shed mass and angular momentum as they settle. Full disruptions approach the canonical fallback law, whereas the late-time slope of partial disruptions is not universal and is set by the debris energy distribution near the surviving core.

new.title: Periodicities of small regular jet deviations in SS433 and their origin
new.summary: Based on the results of spectroscopic observations of SS433 conducted with the 2.5-m telescope at the Caucasian Mountain Observatory between 2020 and 2026, we study the deviations of the moving hydrogen and helium emission lines from their positions as predicted by the kinematic model of the jets' precessional motion. In these deviations, in addition to the previously known periodicities of $13^d.08$, $11^d.27$, $6^d.29$, and $5^d.83$, a new period of $3^d.08$ is identified. All observed periodicities are explained by a model in which the jet offsets occur in a fixed direction relative to the star-disk axis $\bf r$, and the magnitude of the offset is a function $a(\mu)$, where $\mu$ is the cosine of the angle between $\bf r$ and the direction of each jet. The odd terms of the power series expansion of $a(\mu)$ in $\mu$ yield periodicities of $6^d.29$, $5^d.83$, and $3^d.08$, with the jets shifting in opposite directions while remaining parallel. The even powers yield periodicities of $13^d.08$, $11^d.27$, and $4^d.14$ (the latter is not observed), with both jets shifting in the same direction, which was previously misinterpreted as a change in the jets' total velocity $\beta$. With the exception of the $6^d.29$ periodicity, all other displacements occur at an angle of $\approx120^\circ$ to $\bf r$. Superimposed on the regular variability are random deviations (jitter) in the jet directions, independent for the two jets, with $\sigma\lesssim1.\!\!^\circ5$.

new.title: The gravitational wave candidate S251112cm: near-complete optical coverage with ATLAS, Pan-STARRS and the Vera C. Rubin Observatory
new.summary: On 2025 November 12, the LIGO-Virgo-KAGRA (LVK) network detected S251112cm, a compact binary merger candidate with a false alarm rate of one per four years at a luminosity distance of $93 \pm 27$ Mpc. The probability that the lighter component's mass lies below 1 $M_\odot$ is >99%, while the probability that either component lies at 1-3 $M_\odot$ is only 8%, leaving the nature of the progenitor system unclear. We present Pan-STARRS and ATLAS optical follow-up of the 90% localisation region, and quantify Vera C. Rubin Observatory target-of-opportunity observations. In the North, Pan-STARRS imaged 1084 deg$^2$ (65%) within 7 days to a median depth of 21.9 mag and ATLAS 1545 deg$^2$ (87%) within 14 days to 19.3 mag across both hemispheres; in the South, Rubin covered 849 deg$^2$ (36%) 2-10 days post-merger to median depths of 24.5 ($g$) and 23.5 ($i$) mag. They reported 173, 93 and 67 candidates respectively (269 unique), which we assess against AT 2017gfo-like kilonova and SN 1998bw-like broad-lined Type Ic supernova models using prior activity, host luminosity distance, photometric evolution and absolute magnitude. Eight survive, mainly for lack of distance information. Six of these lie in hosts fainter than any in a volume-limited comparison sample, suggesting they are background sources. AT 2025aimy declines too slowly for the AT 2017gfo-like model, and a VLT host spectrum places AT 2025alqe outside the LVK volume, leaving no convincing counterpart candidates. Pan-STARRS and Rubin together exclude both models in $\sim$80% of the 90% localisation volume: the deepest wide-area constraint on a subsolar-mass merger to date and, to our knowledge, the most complete optical coverage of a significant subsolar-mass candidate.

new.title: SN 2017gkk: A moderately luminous and fast evolving Type IIb supernova
new.summary: We present optical imaging (\textit{BVRI} bands) and low-resolution optical spectroscopic follow-up of Type IIb supernova SN~2017gkk that occurred in NGC~2748. These observations consist of 31 and 17 epochs of photometry and spectroscopy, spanning $\sim$\,218 days since the $V$-band peak. The light curve analysis infers that the SN reached maximum in $\sim$\,13~days after the explosion with an absolute magnitude of $M_\mathrm{V}$\,=\,--17.01\,$\pm$\,0.07 mag. The peak pseudo-bolometric luminosity of SN~2017gkk is $L_{\rm bol}=(8.37\pm0.19)\times10^{41}\,\mathrm{erg\,s^{-1}}$. Between 25 and 80 days (after maximum), SN~2017gkk displays a fast decline rate of $2.35\pm0.06~\mathrm{mag\times(100d)^{-1}}$ in $V$-band. The photospheric phase spectra are dominated by an H$\alpha$ P~Cygni profile (up to $\sim$\,69~days), which gradually faded and disappeared $\sim$\,90 days after the $V$-band maximum. The \ion{He}{1} lines subsequently emerged after $\sim$\,20 days and became dominant during the transition phase. The nebular phase spectra of SN~2017gkk indicate a relatively low-mass progenitor with $M_{\mathrm{preSN}}\gtrsim3\,M_\odot$ and $M_{\mathrm{ZAMS}}\approx\,12\,\mathrm{M_\odot}$, and it is likely in a binary system. The analytical modeling of the light curve infers a low ejecta mass of $M_{\mathrm{ej}}=1.38^{+0.48}_{-0.31}\, M_\odot$ with relatively lower explosion energy $E_\mathrm{KE}=0.69_{-0.17}^{+0.25}\times10^{51}\,\mathrm{erg}$ and a synthesized $^{56}$Ni mass of $M_{\mathrm{Ni}}=0.076_{-0.024}^{+0.032}\, M_\odot$.

new.title: Gamma-Ray Pulsar Discovery Using a Lattice-Based Method
new.summary: Pulsars are difficult to discover via $\gamma$-ray pulsations because typically only one photon is observed per ${\sim}10^8$ rotations. We report the first $\gamma$-ray pulsar discovered with an extension of a recently proposed algorithm, which uses efficient tools for identifying short vectors in high-dimensional lattices instead of exhaustively searching for periodic signals. PSR J1622$-$7204, an isolated pulsar spinning at 261 Hz, was found in 15 years of Fermi-LAT data using about ten CPU hours. In contrast, the previous state-of-the-art (a semicoherent search) failed after ${\sim}600$ CPU years. This new approach may enable the discovery of many new $\gamma$-ray pulsars, including in binary systems, a previously intractable problem without detailed prior knowledge of the orbital parameters.

new.title: Multimessenger constraints on the origin of long gamma-ray bursts with plateaus: three cases
new.summary: The central engines of long gamma-ray bursts (LGRBs) with X-ray plateaus remain uncertain. They involve a magnetar or black hole (BH), powered by spin energy and/or accretion. We examine how gravitational waves (GWs) discriminate between these scenarios. For collapsars, we consider three models: (A) a prompt phase powered by hyper-accretion onto a BH, followed by a spin-down-powered plateau; (B) a prompt phase powered by BH spin-down; and (C) a magnetar powering both the prompt and plateau phases. Each predicts a distinct GW signature in timing, energy, and frequency, ranging from broadband emission to a coherent descending chirp. We fit the selected X-ray plateaus of Swift GRBs using the model (A). For GRB~080319C, GRB~111209A, and GRB~130925A, we obtain BH masses of $M_{\rm BH}\sim24$--$124\,M_\odot$, with disc masses of $\sim10\%\,M_{\rm BH}$ at the end of the prompt phase. Mass-scaling of numerical simulations of disc emission yields GW strains of $\sim1.5-1.8\times10^{-24}$ at few hHz. This emission should be detectable by Cosmic Explorer and the Einstein Telescope, with an inferred rate from $0.5$ to $1.5$ yr$^{-1}$. However, ultra-long GRBs powered by tidal disruption events are expected to emit GWs at frequencies ranging from millihertz to decihertz, potentially within the sensitivity range of DECIGO and/or Big Bang Observer (BBO). Current or future detectors may detect GWs associated with BH-powered GRB, but magnetar engines, require next-generation detectors. Current and future detectors could map LGRB central-engine activity.

new.title: Near Infrared HST Images Resolve the Filamentary Emission Knots in Pa 30, the Remnant of the Galactic Supernova of 1181 AD
new.summary: We report the results of a near-infrared HST WFC3/IR imaging program investigating the sub-arcsecond structure of optical filaments in the Galactic nebula, Pa 30, believed to be a SNIax remnant of the historic supernova of 1181 AD. Using a near infrared filter sensitive to [S II] and [S III] emission lines, a 1.2 micron filter to reject stars, and a deep Gemini GMOS [S II] image to help define the remnant's filaments, we identify 226 knots along radially aligned filaments in 15 fields. Knot median PSF-corrected FWHM is 0.154'' (350 AU at 2.3 kpc) with 32 (14%) unresolved at a PSF of 0.225''. We find that Pa 30's knots are not round but elongated along the filaments. Fitting stacks of knots with their axes aligned to their filament directions and calibrating with artificial knots gives intrinsic sizes of 0.18'' along and 0.11'' across filaments, with about 75% of knots longer when measured along the filament. The minimum nearest-neighbor spacing of knots along a filament is typically 0.6'' (1400 AU) so several times their own size, but can be one-arcsecond or larger in places. This results in 5'' to 15'' long discontinuous chains of separate clumps rather than a continuous structure. We find excellent agreement with recent ground-based Gemini images of Pa 30 when HST images are blurred to the 0.5'' Gemini PSF and conclude that filamentary knots detected in Gemini data are actually blurred HST resolved knots. Finally, we give estimates on the density and mass of sulfur in these knots, set an upper limit on their [Fe II] 1.257 micron flux, and briefly discuss implications for modeling the formation of the remnant's filaments.

new.title: Outflow Properties from a Broad Range of GR$ν$RMHD Stellar-Mass Black Hole Accretion Disks
new.summary: The majority of the mass ejected by neutron star mergers comes from accretion disk outflows. Over timescales of seconds, the thermodynamic evolution of the disk and its resultant outflows set the stage for the ejecta properties which manifest in kilonova observations at later times (hours/days). Kilonova observables depend sensitively on key properties of these outflows -- mass ejection, the ejecta velocity distribution, late-time ejecta morphology and nucleosynthetic yields -- which can only be modeled with a detailed treatment of microphysical interactions including neutrino and general relativistic effects. In this work, we present a library of 25 general-relativistic magnetohydrodynamic accretion disks with neutrino transport, to our knowledge the largest to date, spanning a broad range of black hole and accretion disk combinations. From fits to our simulations, we derive analytic estimates of the average ejecta velocity distribution and mass ejection both at simulation end and extrapolated out to the end of the disk's lifetime. We also report ejecta morphology at timescales relevant to kilonova modeling, present spatially-dependent nucleosynthetic yields, and discuss the latter's dependence on initial disk conditions. While our disk library primarily includes initial conditions expected after neutron star mergers, a subset of our disks are applicable to other kilonova-adjacent scenarios.

new.title: Nonlinearly Causal General-Relativistic Superfluid Hydrodynamics: Simulating Vortex Dynamics in Neutron-Star Interiors
new.summary: Neutron stars provide a natural laboratory for superfluid matter under extreme conditions. Its nonlinear dynamics is central to pulsar glitches, their possible links to fast radio bursts, and tidal interactions in inspiralling binaries. We develop a general-relativistic superfluid hydrodynamics framework incorporating entrainment, vortex forces, and line energy, and derive, for the first time, necessary and sufficient conditions for nonlinear causality and strong hyperbolicity. We also show that commonly used dissipative, force-balanced formulations without line tension are generically ill-posed at short wavelengths because of the Donnelly-Glaberson instability. Exploiting the analogy between vortex arrays with tension and force-free electrodynamics, we recast vortex dynamics in terms of effective electric and magnetic fields and drift velocities. This motivates a new finite-volume scheme combining constrained transport of superfluid vorticity with implicit electric-field evolution, enabling stable numerical evolution of the full system. We validate the scheme using an exact solution to the relativistic superfluid Riemann problem and Kelvin-wave dispersion relations, among other tests. Finally, we simulate dynamical, global general-relativistic two-fluid neutron-star equilibria, validate their oscillation modes, and present the first simplified calculation of superfluid interior spin-down with prescribed vortex release and repinning. The resulting stationary state retains both a net twist in the vortex array and residual differential rotation of the superfluid. Our framework thus enables nonlinear numerical studies of general-relativistic superfluid dynamics in neutron-star interiors.

cross.title: Exact ultrastatic multi-throat wormholes: Geometry, energy conditions, and optical cavities
cross.summary: We construct an exactly solvable hierarchy of static, spherically symmetric, wormholes with arbitrary finite throat multiplicity. A factorized prescription for the derivative of the areal radius places every stationary sphere at a prescribed proper distance while retaining elementary integrability and asymptotic flatness. The order-$N$ geometry contains exactly $N+1$ throats and $N$ anti-throats, arranged as an alternating chain of necks and finite interior cavities. Independently of this particular hierarchy, the Einstein equations imply three universal ultrastatic results. Every nondegenerate throat violates the radial null energy condition, whereas every nondegenerate anti-throat satisfies the null, weak, dominant, and strong energy conditions, with the strong-energy sum condition saturated. The same local combination $\rho+p_\ell$ fixes the radial stability of the associated circular null orbit through $V_{\mathrm {null}}''=8\pi L^2(\rho+p_\ell)/\mathcal R^2$; throats are therefore unstable light rings and anti-throats are stable ones. Finally, every finite cell between consecutive stationary spheres, each exterior cell, and the complete two-ended radial null geodesic carry strictly negative integrated radial null energy. The resulting spacetimes are exact multi-cavity optical chains whose cavity centers are locally nonexotic even though no cell can eliminate averaged radial exoticity. The first nontrivial member interpolates continuously from the Ellis-Bronnikov wormhole through a quartically degenerate throat to a double-throat geometry and admits closed expressions for its source, null average, branchwise Morris-Thorne form, embedding criterion, and traversability scales. Its vanishing Arnowitt-Deser-Misner mass follows from the specific radial falloff of the hierarchy, rather than from ultrastaticity alone.

cross.title: Testing the Universality of RAR Model with Constraints on Fermionic Dark Matter for M31
cross.summary: The Ruffini--Argüelles--Rueda (RAR) model describes dark matter as a self-gravitating system of massive fermions in thermodynamic equilibrium within general relativity. It suggests a dual morphology in galaxies: a highly degenerate quantum core mimicking a central supermassive black hole, and a classical halo that explains galactic rotation curves. Earlier applications of the model to the Milky Way restricted the fermion mass to $mc^{2}=48\text{--}345~\text{keV}$, and the orbits of the S-stars around Sagittarius~A$^{\ast}$ (Sgr~A$^{\ast}$) favored $mc^{2}=56~\text{keV}$, whereas a recent thermodynamic stability analysis allows only $mc^{2}\approx194\text{--}387~\text{keV}$. In this work, we apply the RAR model to the Andromeda galaxy (M31), which hosts a dark compact object of approximately $1.4\times10^{8}~M_{\odot}$ within $0.19~\text{pc}$, roughly 33 times the mass of Sgr~A$^{\ast}$. We solve the relativistic equilibrium equations for $mc^{2}=6\text{--}60~\text{keV}$. For all these masses, the fermionic core lies within $0.19~\text{pc}$ and provides the central mass without a black hole. With a bulge and disk added, the total rotation curve is statistically acceptable ($\chi^{2}/N_{\text{dof}}\approx1.18$) but lies below the disk data at $3\text{--}11~\text{kpc}$, an offset attributed to the baryonic models we adopted. The Navarro--Frenk--White (NFW) and Burkert profiles fitted to the same data give a lower $\chi^{2}$ but require an additional black hole. The stability of the M31 core against gravitational collapse limits the fermion mass to $mc^{2}\lesssim60~\text{keV}$. With the earlier Milky Way range, a single fermion can therefore describe both galaxies only for $mc^{2}=48\text{--}60~\text{keV}$, which includes $56~\text{keV}$. With the thermodynamic range, no fermionic core can supply the central mass of M31, so M31 would have to host a black hole.

cross.title: Subsolar neutron star-black hole binaries from collapsars: Gravitational waveform models and detectability in current searches
cross.summary: Detecting subsolar objects in binary mergers would be an exceptional discovery in gravitational wave astronomy. So far, dedicated searches for subsolar coalescences reported no confident detections, setting upper bounds on their merger rate. Given that standard stellar evolution is not able to produce subsolar candidates, a confident detection would point either to new physics or to unconventional astrophysical pathways. These include collapsars, where the outer parts of neutrino-cooled accretion disks around newborn stellar-mass black holes are subject to fragmentation and give rise to subsolar neutron stars, which can later merge with the central black hole. We show that current subsolar searches may miss a significant fraction of these neutron star-black hole mergers, because their templates do not account for the small mass ratios, the tidal disruption of the neutron star, and the effects of the surrounding gas. This result motivates improving the waveform modeling used in current subsolar searches and building adequate template banks tailored to these systems.

cross.title: First $Ω_{\rm m}-w$ Measurement Using Only Fast Radio Burst Observations
cross.summary: Though fast radio bursts (FRBs) are widely advocated as a dark energy probe, no valid $\Omega_m-w$ constraint has been obtained exclusively from FRB data to date. Benefiting from a rapidly growing localized sample and a novel statistical framework for modeling the dispersion measure (DM), we report the first simultaneous inference of the matter density $\Omega_m$ and dark energy equation of state parameter $w$ from FRBs alone, without external observational priors on these two parameters. We combine a multi-parameter emulator for the nonlinear matter power spectrum with a physically motivated electron prescription to construct a cosmology-dependent cosmic-DM distribution. Within this unified analysis framework, the mean and variance of DM respond self-consistently to the same underlying cosmology, directly connecting the FRB likelihood to both cosmic expansion and structure growth. Analyzing 125 localized FRBs at $0.105\leq z\leq2.148$, we obtain $\Omega_m = 0.33^{+0.10}_{-0.11}$ and $w = -0.80^{+0.28}_{-0.38}$ under the flat $w$CDM model. We find a new positive $\Omega_m-w$ degeneracy in the FRB posterior, opposite to the strong anticorrelation derived from Type Ia supernovae, offering a complementary test of dark energy properties and highlighting their potential in future precision cosmological studies.

cross.title: Dark Matter Model Implications of a Candidate Sub-halo Near the Sun, and the Data Needed to Discriminate Among Them
cross.summary: Pulsar-timing accelerations point to a localized mass concentration near the Sun, consistent with a dark matter sub-halo. We work out what such an object implies for the nature of dark matter, organizing the implications by their observable effect: suppression or enhancement of structure formation, internal structure and survival after formation, and emission or scattering by the constituents. We discuss ultralight wave dark matter, thermal and nonthermal warm dark matter, dark acoustic oscillations and dark matter-baryon scattering, elastic and inelastic self-interactions, invisible decays with recoil, primordial black holes, indirect detection, and a possible connection to the LUX-ZEPLIN high-energy recoil candidate. We then ask what new data would discriminate among these models. The existing accelerations are measured outside the tidal radius, where they are blind to the interior mass distribution, to the object's velocity, and to the sub-halo population. We identify four routes that lift these degeneracies: accelerations measured inside the halo, which separate point-mass, cuspy, and cored profiles; lensing and accretion, which test whether the mass is compact; the morphology of annihilation or decay emission, which probes the inner profile; and a search for a comoving stellar population, which tests whether the object is dark and measures its velocity. We also contrast this program with pulsar-timing-array searches for transiting dark matter substructure, which probe vastly lighter objects through a different observable.

cross.title: Impact of Effective Nucleon Mass and Symmetry Energy on Nuclear Pasta Phases and the Unified Equation of State of Neutron Stars
cross.summary: We investigate how the effective nucleon mass and symmetry energy affect pasta phase properties and the unified equation of state (EOS) of neutron stars. The nonuniform pasta structure is described within the self-consistent Thomas-Fermi approximation, while nucleonic interactions are treated in the relativistic mean-field framework with several typical parameter sets adopted. Our results indicate that the symmetry energy and its slope are crucial in determining the onset of pasta phases and their geometric configurations. In the high-density region where matter becomes uniform, the effective nucleon mass plays a dominant role. A larger effective nucleon mass tends to soften the EOS, which yields a smaller radius for a canonical $1.4 M_{\odot}$ neutron star and reduces the corresponding tidal deformability.

cross.title: The Silk Nebula Revisited: A Comment on Wu et al. (2026) and New Constraints from Archival Survey Spectroscopy
cross.summary: Wu et al. (2026) used one LAMOST MRS-N plate to suggest that the Silk Nebula, a $17^\circ$-long \Oiii~$\lambda$5007 filament in Gemini, is possibly associated with a supernova remnant at a fiducial distance of $\sim$160\,pc. We test this against their published values and independent archival data. The \Ni\ airglow in their blue-arm spectrum lies at air, topocentric rest wavelengths, so their \Oiii\ velocities omit the heliocentric correction and are $10.1\pm1.0$\,\kms\ too high. Corrected and combined with DESI DR1 and SDSS spectra, \Oiii\ lies at \vhel\ $=+13.3\pm1.0$\,\kms, the velocity of \Nii\ and of the local warm ionized medium (WIM). Their \Ha\ velocities are 4.5--6.7\,\kms\ redder than \Nii. Their tabulated distances are in kpc, not units of 100\,pc, and kinematic distances carry no information in this direction. Their surface brightness exceeds independent measurements (1.4--2.5 rayleighs) by factors of 4.6--8.6. Their red-line shock criteria are met equally in their nebula-free background region and describe the WIM; their other remnant diagnostics do not constrain the filament. DESI and SDSS spectra show that the filament is Balmer-dark (\Oiii/\Hb\ $>11$) and \Oii-strong, with \ion{He}{2}/\Oiii\ $<0.026$; GALEX shows a coincident ultraviolet ridge, with no \Ha, \ion{H}{1}, dust or X-ray counterpart. These properties, and the lack of an ionizing source, exclude photoionization equilibrium and complete radiative shocks and match a column-truncated radiative shock of $\sim$80--120\,\kms\ seen edge-on, plausibly on the limb of the Monogem Ring at $\sim$250--320\,pc. Far-ultraviolet and deep optical spectroscopy, a two-epoch proper motion and high-ion absorption toward bracketing white dwarfs would be decisive.

cross.title: Self-gravity depletes superradiant clouds
cross.summary: Superradiant clouds of ultralight scalars around black holes are often modeled as free fields, whose levels grow independently and decay slowly through gravitational-wave emission. We show that this limit is never realized. The cloud's self-gravity redistributes particles between levels, just as in the case of axion self-interactions, and dominates over self-interactions for decay constants $f_a\gtrsim6\times10^{16}\,{\rm GeV}\,(\alpha/0.1)$, with $\alpha$ the gravitational fine-structure constant. Self-gravity depletes the cloud by orders of magnitude and feeds more extended levels, weakening all signals that rely on the existence of a large cloud mass. A binary companion, however, can partly offset the depletion. Any assessment of superradiant signals must therefore account for both self-gravity and the cloud's environment.

cross.title: Which black hole modes ring freely? Horizon regularity, the forced ringdown transient, and GW250114
cross.summary: The quasinormal modes (QNMs) of a black hole are defined by keeping only ingoing waves at the horizon. We ask what horizon regularity requires of the outgoing waves this condition discards. For a scalar-like perturbation, bounded first derivatives in a frame regular at the future horizon rule out outgoing waves that decay more slowly than the surface gravity $\kappa$, and smoothness singles out a ladder of frequencies, $\omega=m\Omega_{\rm H}-ij\kappa$ with $j=1,2,\dots$ and $\Omega_{\rm H}$ the horizon angular velocity. We call these the horizon modes. For Schwarzschild black holes and the dominant $\ell=m=2$ Kerr modes, only the fundamental QNM decays more slowly than $\kappa$. These local statements leave the QNM spectrum unchanged but matter for merger ringdowns, because a source falling through the horizon drives the exterior at the horizon frequencies. Each QNM then has a driven and a free part, and the free part takes over only once the driving decays faster than the mode. The fundamental mode separates from the driving early. The overtones stay driven until the source is hidden behind the potential barrier, so overtone amplitudes fitted near the signal peak are in general not those of free oscillations. In GW250114, a ringdown model of the fundamental mode plus the first horizon mode, $\omega=2\Omega_{\rm H}-i\kappa$, is preferred over the fundamental mode plus its first overtone, with Bayes factors between 2 and 30, for start times from $2M_f$ before to $8M_f$ after coalescence. The horizon-mode fit returns a remnant that is heavier and spins faster than the inspiral predicts, as expected from nonlinear backreaction: the horizon that emits the mode has not yet settled to its final mass and spin. Zero-noise injections of numerical-relativity-calibrated waveforms reproduce both the preference and the shift, which are therefore features of general relativity.

repl.title: Science Prospects for the Southern Wide-field Gamma-ray Observatory: SWGO
repl.summary: Ground-based gamma-ray astronomy is now well established as a key observational approach to address critical topics at the frontiers of astroparticle physics and high-energy astrophysics. Whilst the field of TeV astronomy was once dominated by arrays of atmospheric Cherenkov Telescopes, ground-level particle detection has now been demonstrated to be an equally viable and strongly complementary approach. Ground-level particle detection provides continuous monitoring of the overhead sky, critical for the mapping of extended structures and capturing transient phenomena. As demonstrated by HAWC and LHAASO, the technique provides the best available sensitivity above a few tens of TeV, and for the first time access to the PeV energy range. Despite the success of this approach, there is so far no major ground-level particle-based observatory with access to the Southern sky. HESS, located in Namibia, is the only major gamma-ray instrument in the Southern Hemisphere, and has shown the extraordinary richness of the inner galaxy in the TeV band, but is limited in terms of field of view and energy reach. SWGO is an international effort to construct the first wide-field instrument in the south with deep sensitivity from 100s of GeV into the PeV domain. The project is now close to the end of its development phase and planning for construction of the array in Chile has begun. Here we describe the baseline design, expected sensitivity and resolution, and describe in detail the main scientific topics that will be addressed by this new facility and its initial phase SWGO-A. We show that SWGO will have a transformational impact on a wide range of topics from cosmic-ray acceleration and transport to the nature of dark matter. SWGO represents a key piece of infrastructure for multi-messenger astronomy in the next decade, with strong scientific synergies with the nearby CTA Observatory.

repl.title: A Giant Peanut-shaped Ultra-High-Energy Gamma-Ray Emitter Off the Galactic Plane
repl.summary: Ultra-high-energy (UHE) gamma($\gamma$) rays serve as unique probes for investigating new non-thermal astronomical phenomena within the Galaxy and also for studying PeV particle acceleration and propagation. Based on the UHE $\gamma$-ray survey conducted by LHAASO, this paper reports the discovery of a new source distinct from all previously identified high energy $\gamma$-ray objects. This source exhibits an elongated, peanut-like structure, which can be described as a rectangular strip measuring 4.6$^\circ$ in length and 0.45$^\circ$ in width, featuring two bright knots. It is located at a Galactic latitude of $-$17.5$^\circ$, well below the Galactic plane and away from regions rich in UHE sources. The energy spectrum is spatially uniform across the entire region and is well fitted by a power-law model with an index of $-$1.95 and a cutoff at 250 TeV. The highest detected photon energy reaches 760 TeV. Morphological and spectral analyses indicate the presence of a powerful particle accelerator in this region, capable of accelerating particles beyond 1 PeV. An energetic millisecond pulsar (MSP) J0218+4232 is located at the brighter end of this source, with a spatial chance coincidence probability of 3.6*10$^{-4}$, corresponding to 3.4$\sigma$. This suggests that the emission from this region very likely originates from particles accelerated within the MSP wind nebulae, potentially providing the first observational evidence supporting the wind nebulae of MSP as sources of UHE $\gamma$ rays. However, the presence of other hidden accelerators, whether associated with known or entirely new populations of PeVatrons, cannot be ruled out, motivating future multi-wavelength observations.

repl.title: The Wandering Supermassive Black Hole Powering the off-nuclear TDE AT2024tvd
repl.summary: We present an analysis of the spectral energy distribution (SED) of the off-nuclear tidal disruption event (TDE) AT2024tvd during its late-time plateau phase, combining X-ray spectra and UV/optical photometry. Using a fully relativistic, compact accretion disk model with self-consistent inner-disk Comptonization, we reproduce the observed SED without significant residuals. The inferred black hole mass ${\rm log}_{10}(M_{\bullet}/M_\odot) \approx 6.0 \pm 0.2$, and the inferred disk parameters place AT2024tvd within known TDE-disk scaling relations ($L_{\rm bol}^{\rm disk}/L_{\rm Edd} \propto T_{\rm p}^4 \propto M_{\bullet}^{-1}$, $L_{\rm plat} \propto M_{\bullet}^{2/3}$, $R_{\rm out}/r_{\rm g} \propto M_{\bullet}^{-2/3}$). Our results show that: (i) there is no currently detected star cluster or dwarf galaxy associated with the source, down to a mass limit of $\log_{10}(M_{\rm gal}/M_{\odot}) \leq 7.6$; (ii) the black hole is a wandering supermassive, rather than intermediate-mass, black hole; and (iii) the source represents an extreme case of black hole-to-host mass ratio, with $M_{\bullet}/M_{\rm gal} > 3\%$, consistent with a heavily tidally stripped nucleus. The latter aligns with cosmological simulations predicting that surviving host remnants of most wandering black holes should not retain a detectable stellar overdensity when located at small halo-centric distances. We discuss differences with previous analyses of this source and highlight why our modeling approach provides a more physically consistent solution with more reliable parameter inference.

repl.title: Anisotropic hybrid stars: Interplay of superconductivity and magnetic field leading to gravitational waves
repl.summary: Neutron stars, at their cores, are highly dense and, thus, are expected to have a number of exotic processes. This includes a possible phase transition to deconfined quark matter at the core, leading to a hybrid star. The quark matter is expected to additionally be color superconducting. The physics of superconductivity plays an important role in understanding the high density matter in the interiors of neutron/hybrid stars. At their high densities, additionally, both proton superconductivity and neutron superfluidity are expected. We study the effect of superconducting (quark/proton) matter, along with the internal magnetic field, leading to pressure anisotropy within hybrid stars. We aim to probe the effect of superconductivity, especially from color superconducting quarks, on hybrid star structure. We propose new phenomenological model anisotropy profiles within a one-dimensional framework. We model quark matter using the vector interaction enhanced Bag model, and hadron matter with the DD2 equation of state. A Maxwell construction joins both phases. We further investigate the possible observational signatures of these hybrid stars. These include mass enhancement and the possibility of continuous gravitational waves arising from the anisotropy induced deformation, giving us a way to further constrain our model and its physical parameters.

repl.title: GRMHD accretion beyond the black hole paradigm: Light from within the shadow
repl.summary: We present the first three-dimensional general relativistic magnetohydrodynamic simulation of sustained accretion onto a horizonless singularity in which matter reaches the central object rather than being accumulated outside of it or expelled in outflows. We consider a Joshi-Malafarina-Narayan (JMN-1) spacetime, a well-motivated black hole mimicker that arises from gravitational collapse with anisotropic pressure in general relativity, and adopt a compactness parameter for which the central singularity is null. We find that the system evolves into a sustained magnetically arrested disk state. For parameters appropriate to the low-luminosity active galactic nucleus M87*, we obtain an accretion rate of $\sim(3.0 \pm 0.5)\times 10^{-6} \dot{M}_{\rm Edd}$, in full agreement with estimates based on black hole models and, in particular, comparable to that of our reference Schwarzschild black hole simulation. Synthetic ray-traced images at $230\,{\rm GHz}$, computed using polarized general relativistic radiative transfer, are broadly consistent with the Event Horizon Telescope observations of M87*. We identify a key observational discriminant between a black hole and JMN-1: the presence of detectable brightness inside of the ``observable" shadow of JMN-1. This emission originates very close to the central singularity, in a region that would be hidden behind the event horizon in a black hole spacetime. Although this signature is beyond the reach of current observations, it falls within the projected imaging dynamic range of next-generation radio interferometric instruments, offering a robust test of the black hole paradigm.

repl.title: Rapid polarization position angle variations in FRB 20240114A point to a magnetospheric origin
repl.summary: Fast radio bursts (FRBs), thought to originate from magnetars, exhibit diverse polarization properties that constrain their emission physics and local magneto-ionic environments. The polarization position angle (PPA) is particularly sensitive to magnetic-field geometry in the emitting region and propagation effects in the magnetosphere and beyond. In hyper-active repeaters, PPAs are typically stable within bursts and over timescales of hours to days. Here, we present observations of the repeating source FRB~20240114A, which show significant burst-to-burst PPA variations. Using full-Stokes, high-time-resolution observations from the Nançay Radio Telescope (1.1--1.8\,GHz) and the Effelsberg 100-m telescope (1.3--1.5\,GHz) over $\sim1$~year, we measure rotation measures (RMs), polarization fractions, and time-resolved PPAs across 12 epochs. The RMs remain stable, and the emission is predominantly highly linearly polarized, with $\sim81\%$ of bursts showing $L/I > 0.8$, while circular polarization is weaker ($\sim16\%$ with $|V/I| > 0.1$). We find no evidence for Faraday conversion. The PPA exhibits rapid, stochastic variations from milliseconds to hours, spanning $\pm90^\circ$ during two active periods and $\pm50^\circ$ in a third. The distribution of PPA jumps shows that (1) there is no difference in the distribution of jumps on timescales shorter or longer than 1\,s; (2) positive and negative jumps are equally likely; and (3) a jump of $\pm90^\circ$, as expected from, e.g., orthogonal mode jumps, is not more common than any other value. This combination of stable RM, high linear polarization, and extreme PPA variability is not seen in other hyper-active repeaters. These results disfavor emission from a single fixed region and instead suggest multiple emission regions and/or strong magnetospheric and foreground propagation effects, such as plasma lensing.

repl.title: Hybrid Simulations of Proton Acceleration at Oblique High-$β$ Shocks
repl.summary: Collisionless shocks in the intracluster and intergalactic medium (ICM/IGM) are expected to energize both electrons and ions. While electron acceleration is revealed by prominent radio emission, $\gamma$-ray emission from hadronic interactions remains undetected, suggesting that high-$\beta$ (ratio of thermal to magnetic pressure), low-Mach-number shocks cannot accelerate protons efficiently. We present three-dimensional hybrid simulations of quasi-perpendicular shocks with sonic Mach numbers $M_s\sim{3.4{-}17.5}$, focusing primarily on high-$\beta$ conditions representative of cluster environments and including several lower-$\beta$ comparison runs. We find that weak shocks with $M_s\lesssim5$ are consistently inefficient, with $\varepsilon_{\rm CR}\lesssim0.1\%$, while inefficient cases can persist to substantially higher $M_s$ depending on $M_A$ and $\beta$. In contrast, stronger shocks ($M_s \gtrsim 10$) develop clear power-law tails with slopes $q \sim 4.0$ and reach $\varepsilon_{\rm CR} \sim 3\%$. These results suggest that weak, oblique ICM shocks are generally unlikely to accelerate protons efficiently. However, reducing $\vartheta_{B_n}$ to $\sim 45^\circ$ leads to substantially higher acceleration efficiencies, indicating that magnetic obliquity plays a critical role in determining proton acceleration. Our findings provide a microphysical framework for interpreting radio relic observations, whose polarization suggests that electrons are accelerated at oblique shocks, and the absence of cluster $\gamma$-ray detections.

repl.title: Fast Radio Bursts Trace Cosmic Star Formation with Little Delay
repl.summary: The progenitor channels of fast radio bursts (FRBs) remain debated, with a central question being whether their cosmic rate traces star formation promptly or instead follows it with the long time-delay characteristic of compact-binary mergers. We perform a forward-modeling, hierarchical Bayesian analysis of the CHIME/FRB population, jointly fitting the catalog sample, baseband fluences, and localized host redshifts, while self-consistently incorporating the survey selection function through the injection framework. Adopting the classical cosmic star formation history (SFH) with a range of delay-time models, we find that the reconstructed FRB rate robustly tracks the SFH peak. All models exclude characteristic delays $\Delta t_d > 1.0$ Gyr at the 90\% credible level, with inferred median peak offsets in the range $\Delta t_d = 0.1$--$0.3$ Gyr that remain consistent with a prompt, zero-delay origin at the 2$\sigma$ level. This finding disfavors the previously reported multi-Gyr delays, strongly indicating that the central engine is linked to young remnants (likely magnetars) from stellar collapse and, potentially, to the prompt merger of compact objects.

repl.title: Strongly Magnetized Super-Eddington Accretion: How Spin and Accretion Rate Regulate Energy Output and Mass Loss
repl.summary: Strongly magnetized super-Eddington accretion flows power many important astrophysical systems, but how black hole parameters control their output is unclear. We present 30 general relativistic radiation magnetohydrodynamics simulations of super-Eddington magnetically arrested disks onto stellar-mass black holes, varying mass ($M_{\rm BH}= 5, 15, 30\,M_{\odot}$), spin ($a=0.0,0.9$), and accretion rate ($\dot{M}_{\rm acc} \approx 1-2000\,\dot{M}_{\rm Edd}$). We find that black hole spin and accretion rate jointly regulate wind loss rates and energy output efficiencies, while black hole mass has no effect over the mass range studied here. The BH accretes only $7-30\%$ of the mass supplied to the accretion flow, while the rest is expelled in winds. This accretion fraction decreases with mass supply rate and is lower for high-spin systems. Both spin states produce strong magnetically driven outflows. For $a = 0$, the wind kinetic, radiative, and electromagnetic efficiencies are modest and show little variation across the full simulated range of accretion rates. For $a = 0.9$, both wind power and jet power increase super-linearly with $\dot{M}_{\rm acc}$, with the jet power saturating beyond $\dot{M}_{\rm acc} \sim 100\,\dot{M}_{\rm Edd}$. Radiation is strongly beamed along the funnel, with inverse beaming factors exceeding $100$ for high-spin, high-$\dot{m}$ models viewed face-on. Our results establish that rapid BH spin boosts energy-extraction efficiency, while high accretion rate amplifies total power. We provide scaling relations for luminosities, jet power, accretion ratio, and beaming, offering a framework for interpreting observations of ULXs and other super-Eddington systems.

repl.title: JWST Spectroscopy of Type Ia Supernova 2025rbs from Maximum Light to the Nebular Phase
repl.summary: We present JWST observations of the Type Ia supernova (SN Ia) 2025rbs ($D=$14.5 Mpc) at +1, +23, and +84 days after B-band maximum, spanning a wavelength-dependent transition toward the nebular phase. Combined with ground-based optical and near-infrared (NIR) data, our panchromatic spectra (0.4-14 $\mu$m) include the first maximum-light mid-infrared (MIR) spectrum and the earliest MIR spectroscopic sequence of an SN Ia to date. At peak light, the MIR spectrum exhibits a continuum with permitted and forbidden features, including Si II, Ni II, Mg II, and early-emerging [Ni III-IV] and [Ar II-III]. By +23 days the MIR is dominated by forbidden lines with a weak continuum, and by +84 days it is fully nebular, whereas the optical/NIR spectra remain transitional. The nebular spectrum reveals strongly stratified ejecta, with stable Ni concentrated at the lowest velocities, radioactive Co at intermediate velocities but absent within ~2000 km s$^{-1}$, and Ar occupying an outer shell. We detect small-scale substructure in [Ca IV] 3.21 $\mu$m with few-percent amplitudes on a characteristic scale of ~800 km s$^{-1}$, reflecting clumping in composition or ionization. Radiative-transfer calculations at +1 day substantially underpredict the MIR Mg II features (4.6, 9.6, and 13.0 $\mu$m) despite approximately reproducing the NIR Mg II 1.0927 $\mu$m line, suggesting that the relative strengths of the NIR and MIR transitions are sensitive to the treatment of Mg ionization and excitation. These observations demonstrate that MIR spectroscopy beginning near maximum light simultaneously probes the emerging inner ejecta and rapidly fading outer burning products, providing new constraints for explosion and radiative-transfer models.

repl.title: Multipolar neutrino radiation in binary neutron star mergers: Angular structure, rotational variability, and implications for electron fraction
repl.summary: The angular structure and temporal variability of neutrino emission from binary neutron star mergers are characterized using fully general-relativistic simulations with energy-integrated M1 neutrino transport across a representative set of equations of state, total masses and mass ratios. The main analysis is restricted to merger remnants that do not collapse to a black hole within the simulated time intervals. The angle-dependent neutrino energy flux is extracted on a spherical surface outside the remnant and decomposed into spherical harmonics to quantify its multipolar content and evolution. Following the initial post-merger transient, the neutrino radiation flux approaches an axisymmetric configuration dominated by a strong quadrupolar component, producing persistent polar flux enhancement and equatorial suppression due to torus shadowing. The dipolar contribution remains subdominant, indicating the absence of sustained one-sided emission. The degree of anisotropy increases with mass asymmetry and for softer equations of state, reflecting the compactness and morphology of the remnant--disk system. Superimposed on this time-averaged geometry, coherent azimuthal modulations associated with the $m=1$ mode are identified. The associated half frequency, $f_{\mathrm{dom}}/2\simeq0.6$--$0.7\,\mathrm{kHz}$, is compared with local rotation rates in the simulated remnant--disk systems, suggesting a possible dynamical association between the remnant structure and neutrino variability. Finally, we quantify how the same quadrupole-dominated radiation geometry induces a latitude-dependent equilibrium electron fraction. The polar material is driven close to the neutrino-equilibrium target, whereas equatorial material remains systematically more neutron rich and below equilibrium.

repl.title: Exploring the origin of slow-rotating pulsars: Emission from STARS simulated white dwarfs
repl.summary: An increasing number of slow-rotating pulsars and long-period transients have been observed in recent years. The periods of these sources can be significantly longer than typical pulsar sources, ranging from ~ 100 - 1000 s, or even longer. The observed periods and period derivatives predict high magnetic fields, higher than the Schwinger field, when we consider conventional pulsar models of dipole-driven emission from neutron stars. Interestingly, the periods of these sources are consistent with the current observations of white dwarfs (WDs). We explore the possibility of magnetic WDs, simulated using the stellar evolution code STARS, as the origin of some of these unusual pulsar observations. We simulate WDs with enhanced magnetic fields due to accretion after their formation. We also briefly touch on the more exotic possibility of super-Chandrasekhar WDs as the origin for these sources. We find that expanding the parameter space to include the possibility of a WD origin provides an alternate and viable explanation for these unusual observations.

repl.title: High-precision timing of seven binary millisecond pulsars with the European Pulsar Timing Array
repl.summary: Binary millisecond pulsars (MSPs) serve as exceptional astrophysical laboratories for a wide range of astrophysical studies, all of which rely on precise property measurements allowed by pulsar timing. In this paper, we present high-precision timing solutions for seven binary MSPs monitored by the European Pulsar Timing Array. By combining data collected from the five largest radio telescopes in Europe as well as through their coherently combined form, the Large European Array for Pulsars, we achieved phase-coherent timing solutions for all seven pulsars. We conducted a Bayesian timing and noise analysis on the combined data, yielding measurements of astrometric and orbital parameters either for the first time or with broadly improved precision. For PSRs J0125-2327, J1741+1351, and J2043+1711, we determined their distances and transverse velocities from astrometric measurements, and we inferred their masses via Shapiro delay measurements. Additionally, we examined the various contributions to the secular orbital-period variations for PSRs J0125-2327, J1125+7819, and J1741+1351, and we estimated their kinematic distances. For PSRs J0125-2327 and J1741+1351, we detected the signature of annual-orbital parallax in the timing data. This allowed us to derive a strongly favoured, unique solution for the orbital ascending node and inclination angle for PSR J0125-2327 and a tightly constrained ascending node for PSR J1741+1351. Moreover, we used the orbital periods and their derivatives for several binary MSPs to place upper limits on gravitational-wave strain in both the sub-nanohertz and microhertz frequency regimes. Our results show that the orbits of binary MSPs could provide stringent constraints in the microhertz range, thereby possibly complementing standard pulsar timing array analyses in the future.

repl.summary: A recent study shows that incorporating a new term into the thermodynamic potential density, as required by the thermodynamic consistency criterion, can effectively resolve the thermodynamic inconsistency problems of the conventional perturbative QCD model. This additional term plays a crucial role in resolving inconsistencies at relatively low densities and becomes negligible at extremely high densities. Within this revised perturbative QCD model, we find that if we require only that the energy per baryon of up-down ($ud$) quark matter exceeds 930 MeV so as not to contradict the standard nuclear physics, the maximum mass of an $ud$ quark star allowed by the revised perturbative QCD model can reach up to 2.17 $M_{\odot}$. From this perspective, the observed 2.14 $M_{\odot}$ pulsar PSR J0740+6620 may be an $ud$ quark star. However, if we further impose the constraint that the tidal deformability of a 1.4 $M_{\odot}$ $ud$ quark star must be consistent with the GW170817 event, the maximum mass allowed by the revised perturbative QCD model would decrease to no more than 2.08 $M_{\odot}$. Consequently, our results suggest that the compact object with a mass of 2.50-2.67 $M_{\odot}$, as observed in the GW190814 event, cannot be an $ud$ quark star, according to the revised perturbative QCD model.

repl.title: Two-dimensional Pulsar Distance Inference from Nanohertz Gravitational Waves
repl.summary: Pulsar timing arrays (PTAs) are limited in localizing nanohertz continuous gravitational waves (CGWs) by uncertainties in pulsar distances. We introduce a method to infer pulsar distances in two dimensions, using phase information from the pulsar terms of multiple CGW sources. Our approach can enhance distance precision relative to existing one-dimensional distance-inference methods. Using idealized SKA-motivated PTA simulations with prospective pulsar-distance priors, we combine information from five high-SNR CGW sources with known sky positions and luminosity distances. For example, our method achieves subparsec precision for a simulated pulsar at $0.8\,\mathrm{kpc}$ in $40\%$ of realizations, compared with none for the existing one-dimensional method. Such improvements in pulsar-distance precision could facilitate CGW host-galaxy identification and multimessenger observational prospects.

repl.title: Demographics of Off-Nuclear Tidal Disruption Events Powered by Wandering Black Holes
repl.summary: The four recently discovered off-nuclear tidal disruption events (TDEs)---EP240222a, AT2024tvd, AT2025abcr, and AT2023mfm---together with those found serendipitously over past decades (ESO 243-49 HLX-1 and 3XMM J2150-05), reveal a small but robust population of accreting off-nuclear, or ``wandering'' black holes (WBHs). We analyze their demographic properties in comparison to other populations, we find that (i) every event occurs in a massive early-type galaxy within the narrow range $10.7 \lesssim \log_{10}(M_\star/M_\odot) \lesssim 11.1$, a range that very rarely hosts nuclear TDEs; (ii) their radial displacements span $1 \lesssim R_{\bullet}/{\rm kpc} \lesssim 40$, or $0.003 \lesssim R_{\bullet}/R_{200} \lesssim 0.1$; (iii) a stellar counterpart is detected in pre-TDE observations only when located outside the galaxy's half-light radius; (iv) while nuclear TDE hosts are usually isolated, off-nuclear TDEs and quiescent WBHs are more likely to inhabit galaxy groups or clusters. Using the \texttt{ROMULUS} cosmological simulation, we show that all of these follow naturally from hierarchical galaxy formation. We construct the volumetric density of WBHs, $\phi_{\rm WBH}(M_{\star})$, which places the central 68\% of local WBHs in galaxies with $10.7 \lesssim \log_{10}(M_\star/M_\odot) \lesssim 11.3$, explaining (i) and (iv). This WBH distribution can imply a higher off-nuclear than nuclear TDE rate, at these galaxy masses. Their intrinsic radial distribution is Gaussian-like in $\log_{10}(R_\bullet/R_{200})$, consistent with (ii) except for a deficit of sources at the largest separations. Combined with parent-galaxy light, which suppresses counterpart detections at small separations, this distribution also explains (iii). These results show that off-nuclear TDEs are the accreting counterparts of the WBHs long predicted by cosmological simulations, and that they trace large-scale structure.

repl.title: A strongly hyperbolic viscous relativistic hydrodynamics theory with first-order charge current
repl.summary: We extend the first order dissipative relativistic hydrodynamics model of Bemfica-Disconzi-Noronha- Kovtun (BDNK) in order to include the charge number current in full first order expansion with out-of-equilibrium contribution proportional to the evolution equation of the ideal fluid. We obtain a fully second order system of partial differential equation (PDE) that can be casted in a fully conservative way. We analyze the hyperbolicity of this model coupled to Einstein field equations using a newly developed technique that allows for hyperbolicity studies without explicit first order reduction. Furthermore, we identify a frame choice where our formulation is causal, stable and with positive entropy generation for a wide range of equations of state (EoS). Our analysis shows that the inclusion of an out-of-equilibrium correction to the charge current, plays an important role in guaranteeing the strong hyperbolicity and, therefore, the well-posedness of the system.

repl.title: Prospects for multi-messenger discovery of the gravitational-wave background anisotropies via cross-correlation with galaxies
repl.summary: We present new empirically grounded forecasts for the observability of stochastic gravitational-wave background anisotropies assuming a population of stellar-mass compact binary coalescences as its source. We quantified the discovery potential using simulations based on the Euclid Flagship Galaxy Catalogue and LIGO-Virgo-KAGRA observational constraints in combination with detailed theoretical modelling. We considered the multi-messenger cross-correlation with galaxies as well as the gravitational wave-only cross-correlation across observation-time bins. We found that signal-to-noise ratio greater than five is achievable via cross-correlation of a galaxy catalogue that is complete up to limiting magnitude $i < 24.7$ and has redshift uncertainties $\sigma_z = 0.003 (1+z)$ with a gravitational-wave sky map corresponding to 2 years of observation by a third-generation detector network comprising three interferometers. Network configurations with LIGO-Virgo-KAGRA plus up to two third-generation detectors would be limited to moderate signal-to-noise levels, between three and five, except if merger rates are near the upper bound set by observational constraints, in which case the threshold of five would be reached after 4 years. Detectability without the multi-messenger tracer has proven significantly more challenging, with signal-to-noise ratio remaining below three after 10 years. In light of the plans being carried out in the community for ongoing and upcoming galaxy surveys, this work bodes well for the multi-messenger discovery and exploration of the stochastic gravitational-wave background in the era of next-generation observatories such as the Einstein Telescope and Cosmic Explorer.

repl.title: Neutron stars in $f(Q) = Q +ξQ^2$ gravity
repl.summary: Modified theories of gravity based on the symmetric teleparallel framework have recently attracted considerable attention as viable alternatives to General Relativity. In this context, f(Q) gravity, in which the gravitational interaction is encoded in the nonmetricity scalar Q, provides a consistent geometrical formulation that differs from the standard curvature-based description. In this work, we investigate the structure of neutron stars within a family of f(Q) gravity models by employing realistic equations of state, namely FPS, SLy, ENG and MPA1. Using the covariant formulation of f(Q) gravity, we derive the corresponding Tolman-Oppenheimer-Volkoff equations and apply them to model compact stellar configurations. Numerical integration of the field equations provides the mass-radius relations and the maximum masses supported by each equation of state, enabling a direct comparison with current observational constraints. Furthermore, we analyze the behavior of the nonmetricity scalar both inside and outside the stellar object, providing additional insight into the gravitational structure of compact stars in this framework.

repl.title: Kerr-Newman and genuine Kerr black holes in the Bertotti-Robinson magnetic field
repl.summary: We present a spacetime that describes a rotating and charged black hole immersed in an external magnetic (or electric) field which is oriented along the rotational axis. This solution is characterized by four physical parameters, namely the black hole mass $m$, its charge $e$, Kerr-like rotation $a$, and the value of the external field $B$. Such exact solution to the Einstein-Maxwell equations has a surprisingly simple form. Moreover, for $B=0$ it reduces to standard Kerr-Newman metric, while for $m=0$ and $e=0$ we recover the Bertotti-Robinson universe with a uniform (electro-)magnetic field. We also show that the Kerr-BR solution presented in [Phys. Rev. Lett. 135, 181401 (2025)] has a special charge, and we identify a genuine uncharged Kerr black hole immersed in the magnetic field. In the weak-field limit, it gives the Wald solution. We analyze the main physical properties of the new family, namely singularities, horizons, regularity of axes, charges, entropy, and temperature.

repl.title: A Tight Broad-line Width-Luminosity Relation in Little Red Dots and Its Consequence for Virial Black Hole Masses
repl.summary: JWST has uncovered compact high-redshift sources with red, $\sim 5000$ K optical continua and broad Balmer lines, known as "little red dots" (LRDs). Whether these lines trace gas orbiting a massive black hole or electron scattering in a dense, Eddington-limited envelope around a lighter black hole leaves inferred masses spanning $10^{4}$-$10^{8}\,M_{\odot}$. We test both pictures by uniformly refitting public JWST/NIRSpec spectra of 29 LRDs, 15 other JWST broad-line sources, and luminosity-matched SDSS quasars. At fixed $\mathrm{H}\alpha$ luminosity, LRD broad $\mathrm{H}\alpha$ widths have an intrinsic scatter of 0.054 dex ($<0.075$ dex at 95%), less than half that of quasars (0.12 dex), clustering near $1760\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}}$ outside the three brightest sources. Because single-epoch virial masses scale as width squared, they scatter intrinsically by $<0.16$ dex at fixed $\mathrm{H}\alpha$ luminosity, making virial masses and mass functions nearly deterministic restatements of luminosity regardless of the underlying physics. Compared with the Keplerian speed $v_{\rm K}$ at the photosphere of an Eddington-limited envelope, from each source's measured continuum luminosity and temperature, observed widths are 2.5-3.0 $v_{\rm K}$ (2-3$\times$ standard expectations for virial factors $f_{\rm vir}\approx 0.5$-1), with a quarter of the flux above escape speed and no detected continuum-luminosity dependence at fixed $\mathrm{H}\alpha$ luminosity. Bound orbits outside a spherical photosphere thus require sub-Eddington optical luminosities ($\leq 0.10$-0.30 $L_{\rm Edd}$, a requirement specific to spherical photospheres), whereas an Eddington or super-Eddington spherical envelope requires uniform 2-3$\times$ non-gravitational broadening within the $\mathrm{H}\alpha$-emitting gas.
